lessonTitle: Prenatal Screening and Genetic Testing: Screening versus Diagnosis, CVS, Amniocentesis and Predictive Value

blocks.text: A 38-year-old woman at 12 weeks is told that her combined screening test shows a 'high chance' of Down syndrome, 1 in 40. She is frightened and asks whether her baby has the condition. The honest answer is that the test cannot say; it has only changed the odds. Understanding what screening can and cannot tell us is the first skill in prenatal counselling.

blocks.title: Screening test versus diagnostic test
blocks.text: A screening test is offered to a whole population or a large group to identify those at increased risk of a condition; it does not give a definite answer and some results are false positive or false negative. A diagnostic test is used to confirm or exclude the condition in a person with a positive screening result or other indication, and gives a definitive (or nearly so) answer, but is often invasive.

blocks.markdown: **Prenatal screening tests.** These are non-invasive and carry no procedure-related risk of miscarriage. Common examples: (1) **First-trimester combined test** (about 11-13+6 weeks): ultrasound measurement of the **nuchal translucency** (fluid at the back of the fetal neck, increased in Down syndrome and some other conditions) with maternal serum **PAPP-A** and free **beta-hCG**, combined with maternal age to give a risk estimate. In trisomy 21, nuchal translucency and beta-hCG are typically raised and PAPP-A is typically lowered. (2) **Cell-free DNA (non-invasive prenatal testing, NIPT)** analyses fragments of placental DNA in maternal blood from about 10 weeks; it has high sensitivity and specificity for trisomy 21 but is still a screening test. (3) **Second-trimester quadruple test**: maternal serum AFP, hCG, unconjugated oestriol and inhibin A. In Down syndrome, AFP and oestriol tend to be low while hCG and inhibin A are high. (4) The **mid-trimester anomaly ultrasound** (about 18-21 weeks) looks for structural abnormalities.

**Prenatal diagnostic tests.** These sample fetal or placental cells for chromosome or DNA analysis (karyotype, quantitative fluorescence PCR for rapid aneuploidy detection, chromosomal microarray or specific gene testing). **Chorionic villus sampling (CVS)** takes a sample of chorionic villi (placental tissue of fetal origin) through the abdomen or cervix, usually at about 11-13 weeks, so results are available early. **Amniocentesis** withdraws a sample of amniotic fluid, containing fetal cells shed from skin, gut and urinary tract, through the abdomen under ultrasound guidance, usually from about 15 weeks. Both carry a small procedure-related risk of miscarriage (quoted figures differ between centres and over time, in the order of a fraction of a percent to about 1%, and are generally a little higher for CVS than amniocentesis). A limitation of CVS is **confined placental mosaicism**, where the placenta has a chromosome abnormality that the fetus does not; this can occasionally require amniocentesis to clarify. CVS performed very early (before about 10 weeks) has been associated with limb abnormalities.

rows: Small; generally a little higher than amniocentesis
Small; generally somewhat lower than CVS
Fetal cells; lower risk; amniotic fluid AFP can be measured
Confined placental mosaicism; avoid before 10 weeks

blocks.title: Choosing a test after a high-risk screen
blocks.prompt: A woman at 12 weeks has a high-risk combined screening result for trisomy 21 and wants a definitive answer as soon as possible. Which test would you discuss, and what are its trade-offs?

steps.text: The screening result gives only an increased risk. A diagnostic test is needed to confirm or exclude trisomy 21.
At 12 weeks, the options are CVS (available now, within the usual 11-13 week window) or waiting until about 15 weeks for amniocentesis.
CVS provides an earlier result but has a slightly higher miscarriage risk and rarely detects confined placental mosaicism; amniocentesis has a lower risk but a later result.
The woman should be offered non-directive counselling about these trade-offs so she can make an informed choice.

blocks.answer: CVS is usually the option for an early diagnosis, with a small procedure-related risk and the possibility of placental mosaicism; amniocentesis is the alternative, with later timing.

blocks.markdown: **Interpreting test results: sensitivity, specificity and predictive value.** For a screening test applied to a population: **sensitivity** is the proportion of affected pregnancies that test positive; **specificity** is the proportion of unaffected pregnancies that test negative. The **positive predictive value (PPV)** is the probability that a person with a positive test truly has the condition, and it depends strongly on the **prevalence** of the condition in the group tested. Even an excellent test has a modest PPV when the condition is rare, because the false positives from the large unaffected group outnumber the true positives.

blocks.caption: Positive predictive value; TP = true positives, FP = false positives.

blocks.title: Positive predictive value of a screening test
blocks.prompt: A screening test has sensitivity 90% and specificity 95%. The condition has a prevalence of 1 in 500. What is the PPV, and how should the result be explained to a woman with a positive result?

steps.text: True positives = 0.90 x 200 = 180. False positives = 0.05 x 99,800 = 4,990.
Only about 3.5% of positive screens are truly affected. This is why a positive screening test must be followed by a diagnostic test.

blocks.answer: PPV is about 3.5%; most positive screening results are false positives, so a diagnostic test is needed to confirm.

blocks.title: Predictive value depends on prevalence
blocks.text: Sensitivity and specificity are properties of the test, but PPV also depends on how common the condition is in the group tested. The same test has a higher PPV in a high-risk group (for example older mothers) than in a low-risk group. A negative result from a high-sensitivity screening test makes the condition less likely but does not rule it out.

items: Screening estimates risk, non-invasively; diagnostic tests give a definitive result but are invasive.
Combined test: nuchal translucency, PAPP-A and free beta-hCG at about 11-13 weeks; NIPT is also screening.
CVS (about 11-13 weeks, placental tissue) versus amniocentesis (from about 15 weeks, amniotic fluid).

blocks.title: Counselling
blocks.text: A positive NIPT or combined screening result is not a diagnosis. Counselling should be non-directive, and the choice to have an invasive test, or no test, belongs to the woman. Say which result type you are discussing: risk, not diagnosis.

points: Screening tests estimate risk and are non-invasive; diagnostic tests (CVS, amniocentesis) confirm or exclude the condition but carry a small miscarriage risk.
CVS is done at about 11-13 weeks on placental tissue; amniocentesis from about 15 weeks on amniotic fluid; CVS can show confined placental mosaicism.
PPV depends on sensitivity, specificity and prevalence, so a positive screen for a rare condition is often a false alarm.

questions.stem: Which statement best distinguishes a screening test from a diagnostic test?

options.text: A screening test estimates risk in many people, whereas a diagnostic test confirms or excludes the condition in an individual
A screening test is always invasive, whereas a diagnostic test is non-invasive
A screening test gives a definitive diagnosis, whereas a diagnostic test gives only a risk
A screening test can be done only in the first trimester

questions.correctOptionText: A screening test estimates risk in many people, whereas a diagnostic test confirms or excludes the condition in an individual

distractorRationale.a: Correct: screening identifies increased risk, diagnosis confirms.
distractorRationale.b: This is reversed: screening is usually non-invasive and diagnostic tests such as CVS are invasive.
distractorRationale.c: Screening gives only a risk; it is not definitive.
distractorRationale.d: Screening tests are done in both trimesters, e.g. the quadruple test in the second.

questions.explanation: Screening tests, such as nuchal translucency with serum markers, give a risk estimate for a population and have false positives and negatives. Diagnostic tests, such as CVS or amniocentesis, give an answer for the individual pregnancy.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a prenatal diagnostic rather than a screening test?

options.text: Karyotyping of cells from amniotic fluid
Cell-free fetal DNA analysis in maternal blood

questions.correctOptionText: Karyotyping of cells from amniotic fluid

distractorRationale.a: Correct: analysing fetal cells directly gives a definitive chromosomal result.
distractorRationale.b: The quadruple test is a screening test.
distractorRationale.c: Nuchal translucency is part of screening.
distractorRationale.d: NIPT is a screening test, not diagnostic, as it analyses placental DNA fragments in maternal blood.

questions.explanation: Karyotyping fetal cells obtained by amniocentesis directly examines the fetal chromosomes and is diagnostic. The other options estimate risk and require confirmation.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old woman is at 18 weeks' gestation with a high-risk screening result and has not had a diagnostic test. Which procedure is appropriate at this gestation to obtain fetal cells for chromosome analysis?

options.text: Chorionic villus sampling, which is performed only before 10 weeks
Maternal serum AFP alone, which is diagnostic

distractorRationale.a: Correct: amniocentesis is performed from about 15 weeks, so it is suitable at 18 weeks.
distractorRationale.b: CVS is usually done at about 11-13 weeks, and early CVS before 10 weeks is discouraged, so it is not the method at 18 weeks.
distractorRationale.c: Serum AFP is a screening marker, not diagnostic.
distractorRationale.d: The nuchal translucency can be measured only in the first trimester window and is a screening test.

questions.explanation: At 18 weeks the usual diagnostic option is amniocentesis, which samples fetal cells in the amniotic fluid. Nuchal translucency and maternal serum markers are screening tests and cannot confirm a diagnosis.

questions.stem: A CVS sample shows trisomy 21 in some cells and a normal karyotype in others, while the fetal ultrasound is normal. Which explanation is most appropriate, and what is the next step?

options.text: Possible confined placental mosaicism; amniocentesis is offered to examine fetal cells
Definite Down syndrome in the fetus; no further testing is needed
A laboratory error; the result should be ignored
Maternal contamination only; the mosaic result is always irrelevant

questions.correctOptionText: Possible confined placental mosaicism; amniocentesis is offered to examine fetal cells

distractorRationale.a: Correct: the placenta can differ from the fetus, so a second sample from fetal cells clarifies.
distractorRationale.b: A mosaic CVS result does not prove the fetus is affected.
distractorRationale.c: Mosaic findings are a recognised phenomenon and should not be ignored.
distractorRationale.d: Maternal cell contamination can occur but cannot be assumed to explain a mosaic result.

questions.explanation: CVS samples placental tissue, which can have a chromosome abnormality absent from the fetus (confined placental mosaicism). Amniocentesis samples fetal cells and helps determine whether the fetus is affected.

questions.stem: A cell-free DNA test for trisomy 21 has sensitivity 99% and specificity 99.5% (illustrative values). It is applied in a group in which the prevalence of trisomy 21 is 1 in 200. What is the positive predictive value? Give your answer as a percentage (%).
questions.explanation: Take 100,000 women: 500 affected and 99,500 unaffected. True positives = 0.99 x 500 = 495; false positives = 0.005 x 99,500 = 497.5. PPV = 495 / (495 + 497.5) = 0.499, about 50%. About half of positive results are therefore false positives even for this excellent test, so confirmation with a diagnostic test is advised.

questions.stem: A screening programme tests 40,000 pregnancies for a condition with prevalence 1 in 400. The test has a specificity of 98%. How many false-positive results are expected? Give your answer as a number of women.
questions.explanation: Affected pregnancies = 40,000 / 400 = 100, so unaffected = 39,900. The false-positive rate is 1 - specificity = 0.02, so false positives = 0.02 x 39,900 = 798. This shows how many unaffected women must be counselled after a positive screen.

questions.stem: True or false: A positive result on a non-invasive cell-free DNA screening test for trisomy 21 is a definitive diagnosis and requires no confirmation.
questions.explanation: Cell-free DNA analysis detects placental DNA fragments and is a screening test with false positives, so a positive result should be confirmed by a diagnostic test such as CVS or amniocentesis.

questions.stem: Explain the difference between a screening test and a diagnostic test in prenatal care, giving one example of each, and explain how you would counsel a woman who has a high-risk screening result.
markingGuide: Screening identifies increased risk in a population; non-invasive; no definite answer; false positives and negatives.
Examples: combined test (nuchal translucency, PAPP-A, beta-hCG), quadruple test or cell-free DNA.
Diagnostic test confirms or excludes the condition; invasive; small risk of miscarriage; examples CVS or amniocentesis with karyotype/QF-PCR/microarray.
A high-risk result is not a diagnosis; offer diagnostic testing with non-directive counselling and the option to decline.
Explain risks, timing and limitations of the procedure.
questions.explanation: Screening changes the probability of disease but does not establish it; confirmation needs a diagnostic test. Counselling must explain this and support an informed choice.

questions.stem: A woman with a high-risk first-trimester screening result is considering CVS and amniocentesis. Compare them for timing, tissue sampled, risks and limitations.
markingGuide: CVS about 11-13 weeks; amniocentesis from about 15 weeks.
CVS samples chorionic villi (placenta); amniocentesis samples amniotic fluid containing fetal cells.
Both invasive with small procedure-related miscarriage risk, generally a little higher with CVS.
CVS limitation: confined placental mosaicism (placental result may differ from fetus); very early CVS associated with limb defects.
CVS gives earlier results; amniocentesis later but lower risk.
questions.explanation: The choice balances earlier results (CVS) against slightly lower risk and fetal-cell sampling (amniocentesis).

questions.stem: A test for a fetal condition has sensitivity 95% and specificity 98%. Explain, without calculation, why its positive predictive value will be much lower when the condition has a prevalence of 1 in 1000 than when the prevalence is 1 in 20, and what this means for counselling after a positive result.
markingGuide: PPV is the proportion of positive results that are true positives.
Sensitivity and specificity are properties of the test and do not change with prevalence.
When prevalence is low the unaffected group is very large, so even a small false-positive rate generates many false positives relative to true positives.
When prevalence is higher true positives form a bigger share of positives so PPV is higher.
Counselling: a positive screen in a low-prevalence group is more likely to be a false positive; confirmatory diagnostic testing is needed.
questions.explanation: PPV combines test performance with prevalence. In a rare condition the false positives swamp the true positives, so most positive results are not truly affected.
